newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria's Vranitzky bids farewell as party head.
newsitem.headline: Austria's Vranitzky bids farewell as party head.

text.p: Former chancellor Franz Vranitzky stepped down as head of Austria's Social Democrats on Wednesday, welcoming his successor Viktor Klima and warning of the dangers posed by the popular far-right.
Vranitzky, 59, was visibly moved as, after 11 years in the political spotlight, he took his leave in a speech at the party's annual conference.

"I am confident the party is in good hands. I am sure you will take the party to its next high," Vranitzky told Klima, who is a close personal friend and almost certain to be voted in as the next party leader later on Wednesday.
Vranitzky took the Alpine nation by surprise when he announced his resignation as chancellor and party chief in January and passed the reigns to his finance minister Klima,.
However, until Wednesday he was still technically leader of the Social Democratic Party, which together with the conservative People's Party have dominated the country's political scene since 1945.
Klima admitted that Vranitzky's was a hard act to follow.

"Dear Franz, you have turned Austria into a modern country of high employment, high social standards and achieved our integration in the European Union. We will never forget it," he said, his voice trembling.
"You left the party with no scandals, but with clear support for democracy and clear words against fascism and the extreme right," he added.
The two hugged to loud applause from the floor.
Setting out the agenda for his heirs, Vranitzky said one of their prime goals should be to snatch back votes lost to Joerg Haider's far-right Freedom Party.
"We want to win the votes back not by copying Haider's policies, but by convincing people his is not the right way forward," he said in his speech.
Vranitzky has been widely criticised for having failed to take seriously the growing popularity of the far right under the leadership of the charismatic Haider.

Vranitzky and Haider took over their respective parties within months of each other in 1986. While the Social Democrat vote slumped to an all-time low in European elections last October, dipping below 30 percent, support for the far right soared to nearly 28 percent.

Taking stock of his period in office, the avuncular former chancellor who now serves as the Organisation for Security and Co-operation Europe's envoy to Albania, said Austria's entry to the European Union in 1995 had been one of the high points of his career.
He also drew attention to his efforts to reconcile Austrians to their sensitive wartime past as part of Hitler's Third Reich.
In a visit to Israel in 1993 Vranitzky said Austrians too had to share responsibility for the Nazi Holocaust.
"We have managed to find a new, more relaxed and above all more honest relationship to our past," he said.
But, he warned, no one must forget how National Socialism came about as the threat of extremism was still very real.
"The signs are there, let us not ignore them. If we play down those times it will bring us very quickly back to where we once were," he said.
